llm_major: The rq2 evidence on quality is mostly EFL language proficiency (10.1007/s44217-025-00602-7, a Grammarly tool; 10.3389/fpsyg.2023.1260843, EFL students not necessarily graduate) or self-reported perceptions (10.46303/jcsr.2024.4, 10.54855/ijaile.25212), so argumentation, rigor and originality are effectively unanswered, yet the conflict is framed as improving vs harming 'graduate students' academic writing quality'.
llm_minor: The consensus claim that iterative, collaborative interaction goes with better writing than passive use cites 10.1111/ejed.12824, which only describes metacognitive strategies and measures no writing outcome. 10.1007/s12528-025-09444-6 is also cited without a stated outcome difference.

The first conditional claim says benefits depend on critical evaluation of AI output and on high AI literacy, but 10.1007/s40593-024-00454-6 is a perception interview study with no measured quality outcome, so the moderator is not tied to a measured effect.

The discipline conditional pairs a general-student German survey (10.1057/s41599-023-02304-7, usage by field) with a US course study on AI literacy (10.1016/j.caeo.2024.100184); neither links discipline or exposure to research productivity or quality, so it is not a moderator of effects.

The rq5 consensus on hallucinated citations, integrity and overreliance rests on perceptions and two narrative reviews (reliability 2), and no cited study measures skill erosion or citation fabrication in graduate research.

The coverage_note ends with a stray '}' character, and it concedes that rigor, originality, coding, data analysis and supervisor or policy effects have no evidence, so the brief gives no direct answer for part of rq2, rq3 and rq4.
actions: search rq2: empirical studies of graduate or doctoral students' AI-assisted thesis, proposal or manuscript writing with expert-rated or rubric-scored argument quality, rigor or originality

rationale: Added new queries only for rq2 and rq5, the flagged sub-questions that need more evidence. rq2 now targets rubric-scored or expert-rated quality outcomes in graduate writing, and rq5 targets citation-fabrication audits and measured skill erosion or overreliance. The other critic issues concern synthesis wording and need no new searches.

llm_major: rq1 passes on count but is effectively unanswered: the cited papers (10.3991/ijep.v14i3.48395, 10.46303/jcsr.2024.4, 10.1007/s40593-024-00454-6) report only perceived usefulness, and 10.3390/higheredu2040037 is an n=1 undergraduate case, so none measures writing speed, time saved or publication output.
llm_minor: The first consensus claim cites 10.2196/80371, a GPT-4o reference-fabrication test with no student sample, as support for how graduate students use GenAI, and its 'widespread' use rests on mixed or general student surveys (10.1057/s41599-023-02304-7, 10.1186/s41239-024-00453-6).
Coding and data-analysis use is acknowledged as uncovered, but no paper in the table addresses it, so the gap rests on absence of evidence rather than on a targeted search.

Findings from 10.1016/j.chbah.2024.100095 (AI-augmented writing improved readability but lacked research details and reflective insight) and 10.35542/osf.io/x3dct (AI reviews rated slightly below peer reviews) bear on rq2 quality and originality but are not used in any claim.

The third gap says the evidence conflicts on critical appraisal, but the contrast between 10.1186/s40561-025-00384-3 (appraisal lowered self-efficacy and output quality) and the qualitative studies is not listed in the conflicts section.

llm_major: rq1 is effectively unanswered: no paper in the table measures writing speed, time-on-task or publication output. The only productivity signals are self-reports (10.14742/ajet.8843, 10.3991/ijep.v14i3.48395, 10.46303/jcsr.2024.4) and an n=1 undergraduate autoethnography (10.3390/higheredu2040037).
llm_minor: The conditional claim that better writing performance is associated with high AI literacy and critical engagement cites 10.1111/ejed.12824, which studies metacognitive strategies and not measured writing quality. The 10.1007/s12528-025-09444-6 abstract also does not say which interaction pattern performed better.

The consensus that a substantial share of LLM-generated references are fabricated cites 10.2196/53164 and 10.2196/80371, whose abstracts give no numeric results. The quantitative support comes only from 10.2196/52935 (GPT-3.5, 10 topics).

The cautious consensus merges two different constructs, AI-augmented writing quality rated by 17 HCI reviewers (10.1016/j.chbah.2024.100095) and AI-generated versus peer review feedback (10.35542/osf.io/x3dct). It then treats them as converging evidence on AI-assisted research writing.

The critical-appraisal conflict compares a survey measuring perceived output quality and self-efficacy with qualitative studies (10.1007/s40593-024-00454-6, 10.1093/applin/amaf022, 10.14742/ajet.8843) that report no comparable outcome. The hypothesis refers to 'rated' writing quality that those studies do not provide, so the conflict is partly constructed from non-comparable constructs.

No paper in the table addresses graduate students' use of GenAI for coding, statistical or data analysis, or literature search and review workflows. rq3 is therefore covered only for writing, brainstorming and paraphrasing.

Academic integrity violations, overreliance and skill erosion rest on perception surveys, commentaries and one small qualitative study (10.54855/ijaile.25212), with no graduate-specific empirical evidence on skill erosion or detected misconduct.
The proposed no-access RCT for the productivity gap is hard to enforce, since control-arm students can easily use GenAI elsewhere, and the design does not address contamination.
